title: You Are the Variable
description: What you believe about your power to reach students, and about the power of a team, shapes what happens in your classroom. That belief can be built.
objectives: Define teacher self-efficacy and collective efficacy, and explain why both matter for student outcomes.
Recognize high-efficacy and low-efficacy responses in classroom scenarios.
Describe two strategies for emotional resilience on a hard day and one for staying flexible when a plan fails.
Name your own efficacy starting point and one concrete next step, using your persona's watch-for.

blocks.text: Hard days in teaching are a sign that the work matters. What separates teachers who grow through them from teachers who stall is often not talent. It is what they believe they can do next. This section gives you the research behind that belief, two tools for hard days, and a plan you will revisit before your first evaluation period. It also reinforces ideas from Section 4: self-efficacy, self-regulation, and motivation all appear on the Praxis PLT.

blocks.title: Your plan for the 60 minutes
blocks.text: Content and required reading (33 min), knowledge check (10), mindset check (5), final task (15).

Not graded. Rate how much you agree with each statement right now. You will rate the same statements again after the knowledge check. Your Hard-Day Plan and both sets of ratings become a baseline you will revisit before your first evaluation period.

statements.text: My specific actions can change how a struggling student does.
When a lesson fails, I can figure out what to adjust and try again.
Asking for help is part of taking ownership of my growth.

blocks.text: **Self-efficacy** is a person's belief in their capacity to produce outcomes through their specific actions. It is confidence about a particular situation, such as “I can get this class to understand fractions,” and goes beyond general confidence. The idea comes from psychologist Albert Bandura, whom you met in Section 4.

Teachers with high self-efficacy tend to set more challenging goals, persist longer when students struggle, and recover faster when a lesson goes wrong. Teacher quality matters enormously for students, and what a teacher believes about their own power is part of that. John Hattie's *Visible Learning*, a synthesis of hundreds of meta-analyses, is a common starting point for this research.
Efficacy is built, not found
No resident is expected to arrive with high efficacy in every area. Bandura described four sources that build it, and each shows up in the residency:

rows: Mastery experiences
Succeeding at something real and hard enough to matter
Co-teaching, small-group practice, your first successful reteach
Observing others
Watching someone like you succeed
Classroom visits and videos of mentor teachers
Feedback and encouragement
Specific, credible words from someone who has seen your work
Coaching conversations and evaluation feedback
Managing your state
Reading stress and nerves as information, and steadying yourself
Your hard-day routine, later in this section

blocks.title: Doubt is information, not a verdict
blocks.text: Feeling unsure about a part of teaching you have not done yet does not mean you are unsuited to it. It tells you where to look for practice, a model, or feedback.

Each scenario shows a real classroom situation twice, once with a high-efficacy response and once with a low-efficacy response. **High-efficacy responses** are persistent, reflective, and oriented toward growth. **Low-efficacy responses** are often subtle: giving up quickly on a struggling student, avoiding feedback conversations, or defaulting to blame when a lesson does not land. Recognizing a low-efficacy response in yourself is the first step toward changing it.
Scenario 1: Ms. Rivera
Her class scores lower than she expected on the mid-year assessment. Watch both responses.

blocks.text: **Collective efficacy** is a team's shared belief in its ability to produce positive outcomes for students together. Where self-efficacy is “I can,” collective efficacy is “we can.” In Hattie's research it has one of the highest effect sizes he reports (d = 1.57, compared with an average of 0.40 for all influences in education). In a summary by Donohoo, Hattie, and Eells (2018), it was described as more than three times as powerful as socioeconomic status in predicting student achievement, and stronger than home environment and parental involvement.

Collective efficacy is not about making teachers feel good. It is built through four things: **shared goals**, **shared language**, **shared accountability**, and **repeated evidence** that the team's efforts are making a difference. Evidence of impact is the primary input: a team that sees its students grow starts to believe it can make them grow.

As a resident, you both contribute to and draw from the collective efficacy of your school. Bring your student data and your questions to your team, and notice when a colleague's idea works for your students too.

blocks.text: A hard-day routine in four steps

items: **Name what is happening.** “I am overwhelmed, and my last class went badly.”
**Steady yourself.** Take a slow breath, drink water, step outside for two minutes, or reset your shoulders before the next class.
**Ask for support.** Text your mentor, find a colleague at lunch, or book time with your coach.
**Take one next step.** Pick one small action for tomorrow, such as reteaching one skill or opening class with a clearer routine.

blocks.text: When a plan fails, stay flexible

Flexible teachers do three things: **diagnose** what happened (was the task too hard, the directions unclear, the timing off?), **adjust**, and **try again**. A failed lesson is information about the plan, not a verdict on you.
Your persona's watch-for is a flexibility prompt
In Section 2 you saw a “watch for” note with your persona. Each one tells you where flexibility will matter most for you.

rows: Emcee
Entertainment can crowd out learning.
Build in quiet reflection and independent work so students can process.
Anchor
Routine can harden into a rut.
Add a spark of novelty or a change of pace when students need it.
Engineer
Some moments call for setting the plan aside.
Leave room in the lesson for relationships and real-time needs.
Coach
Not every student responds to pressure or competition.
Personalize the push to each student's pace and needs.
Nurturer
Do not carry every burden alone.
Set gentle, firm boundaries that sustain your care over time.

blocks.text: Every resident enters the year with a different efficacy profile, with areas of genuine strength and areas of anticipated doubt. Both are useful. Naming where you feel capable and where you expect to struggle is the first step toward targeted growth. The residency builds efficacy through deliberate practice, frequent feedback, and a team that has done this work. When doubt shows up, the high-efficacy response is to name it, seek support, and take one concrete next step.
Quick check: where do you feel capable right now?
Rate each area from 1 (not yet confident) to 5 (very confident). This is for you, ungraded, and it helps you write your plan.
Professional growth sources
Professional growth is part of the role, and seeking help when you need it is part of taking ownership of it. Choose the source that fits the need.

rows: Coach
Specific feedback on your own practice
An observation of your directions, followed by one next step
Workshop
Learning a new skill or strategy
A session on questioning techniques you can try the next day
Professional learning community
Solving a shared problem with colleagues and student data
A grade-level team analyzing a common assessment
Professional organization
The wider field, standards, and a network beyond your school
A national or state teaching association for your content area or grade band

questions.prompt: How does John Hattie's Visible Learning research describe the role of teacher self-efficacy?

options.text: It primarily affects teacher job satisfaction, not student outcomes
It is one factor among many, roughly equal in importance to curriculum and school funding
It is one of the most powerful predictors of student achievement identified across more than 1,700 studies
Its effect on student outcomes is limited to students in early elementary grades

questions.explanation: Across 1,700+ studies, teacher self-efficacy stands out as one of the strongest predictors of achievement.

questions.prompt: A teacher's class scores lower than expected on a mid-year assessment. Which response best reflects high self-efficacy?

options.text: "I'll mention this to my coach but keep doing what I'm doing. One assessment isn't everything."
"The assessment probably wasn't a fair measure of what I taught."
"I need to look at where the gaps are and adjust my approach for the next unit."
"These students just aren't putting in the effort. I can't make them care."

questions.explanation: High efficacy means owning the result and adjusting your own practice.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between self-efficacy and collective efficacy?

options.text: Collective efficacy is another term for school culture and has no specific definition in research
Self-efficacy decreases as teachers gain experience; collective efficacy increases
Self-efficacy applies to teachers; collective efficacy applies only to school leaders
Self-efficacy is about believing you can impact outcomes on your own; collective efficacy is a team's shared belief in its ability to produce results together

questions.explanation: Self-efficacy is individual belief; collective efficacy is a team's shared belief.

questions.prompt: According to Hattie's research, collective efficacy has an effect size higher than which of the following factors?

options.text: Student access to technology in the classroom
Class size and student-to-teacher ratio
Teacher credentials and certification status
Socioeconomic status, prior student achievement, and home environment

questions.explanation: Collective efficacy outranks socioeconomic status, prior achievement, and home environment.

questions.prompt: A resident teacher struggles in the first few weeks and begins to think, "Maybe I'm just not cut out for this." Which of the following best reflects a high-efficacy response to this moment?

options.text: Push through independently and avoid showing vulnerability to colleagues or coaches
Focus only on lessons that are going well to rebuild confidence before addressing areas of struggle
Name the doubt, seek support from your coach or team, and identify one concrete next step
Accept that some people are natural teachers and others are not, and adjust expectations accordingly

questions.explanation: Name it, seek support, take one concrete next step.
